lessons.title: Column vectors and journeys
lessons.summary: Read a column vector, reverse a displacement and combine horizontal and vertical components.
lessons.objective: Read a column vector, reverse a displacement and combine horizontal and vertical components.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to read a column vector, reverse a displacement and combine horizontal and vertical components.
lessons.ideas:
A column vector records two signed moves. The top entry is the horizontal move and the bottom entry is the vertical move.

Add or subtract matching entries. Scaling multiplies both entries by the same number.

Two column vectors are equal exactly when both matching entries are equal.
lessons.method:
Start on a set of axes. Count one component at a time. Positive horizontal means right and positive vertical means up. The figure draws the separate moves as dotted lines. The arrow connects the same starting and finishing points. \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) goes from A to B. \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) returns from B to A and has both signs reversed. The numbers in the vector describe the move, so a copy of the same arrow starting elsewhere describes the same vector.

Draw the first arrow. Put the tail of the next arrow at the first arrowhead. The resultant runs from the initial tail to the final arrowhead. A negative multiplier reverses direction as well as changing size. To subtract, put the arrow in reverse before adding it. On paper, draw the arrows first when their order is easy to confuse. Multiply any scalar before adding or subtracting the two columns.

Copy the two columns on opposite sides of the page. Read across each row to build two scalar equations. If a row has no unknown, it gives a quick check of signs. In a journey, the same comparison works for the initial position plus a number of equal displacements. After finding a parameter in one row, put it back into the other row before you finish.
mistakes: The bottom entry gives a vertical displacement. It only gives a y-coordinate when the arrow starts at the origin.
Multiplying only one component will usually change the angle. Keep the same scale factor in both components.
Adding the two components together does not test equality. Equal totals can come from different arrows.

examples.title: End position minus start position
examples.question: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}9\\-5\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
examples.solution:
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}9\\-5\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-5\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-5\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Combine two directions
examples.question: Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}10\\-5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\12\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(5\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).
examples.solution:
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}50\\-25\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}-6\\12\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}56\\-37\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Match the bottom components
examples.question: \(\begin{pmatrix}15\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(2\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\20\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}32\\-40\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).
examples.solution:
The bottom entry gives \(2p-(20)=-40\).

Add \(20\) and divide both sides by \(2\).

Answer: \(-10\).

lessons.title: Magnitudes and unit vectors
lessons.summary: Use a right triangle to find a magnitude, a direction vector of length one or a required signed component.
lessons.objective: Use a right triangle to find a magnitude, a direction vector of length one or a required signed component.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to use a right triangle to find a magnitude, a direction vector of length one or a required signed component.
lessons.ideas:
The two components form the perpendicular legs, so the length rule is \(\left|\mathbf v\right|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\).

Divide by the magnitude to make the length one: \(\widehat{\mathbf v}=\frac{\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|}\).

Scale a unit direction by the requested length. If one component is missing, solve for its square and use the direction to choose its sign.
lessons.method:
Mark the legs parallel to the axes. A leg length is always positive, even when the arrow points left or down. Squaring already removes a negative sign, provided it is inside brackets. Keep exact square roots for surds. The denominator in the normalising factor in the next model is this same length.

Question asks forUseful operation
The displacement between two pointsFinish minus start: \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}\)
The length of a vector\(\left|\mathbf v\right|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\)
A unit vector in the same direction\(\widehat{\mathbf v}=\frac{\mathbf v}{|\mathbf v|}\)

The vector from its tail to its tip points in the required direction. Find its magnitude with Pythagoras. Dividing by that positive length scales the arrow down or up to unit length. Keep two exact fractions in the column vector. Check the result by squaring and adding the two new entries. The basis vectors \(\mathbf i\) and \(\mathbf j\) are unit vectors along the positive horizontal and vertical axes.

For a reverse calculation, put the length squared on one side and both squared components on the other. Isolate the square of the unknown. Both square-root signs are possible until a direction restriction fixes one. When a full direction is given, the unit-vector method avoids working with the two signs separately.
mistakes: Adding the two component lengths gives a route along the sides of the triangle. The vector length runs across the diagonal.
A vector of length one can point in any direction. Check the signs against the original arrow.
The magnitude does not distinguish upward from downward. Read the stated sign or quadrant before deciding.

examples.title: Measure the length of an arrow
examples.question: Find the magnitude of \(\begin{pmatrix}-154\\-528\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
The legs of the component triangle have lengths \(154\) and \(528\).

The square of the length is \(-154^2+(-528)^2=302500\).

Take the positive square root.

Answer: \(550\).

examples.title: A unit vector in the same direction
examples.question: Find a unit vector in the direction of \(\begin{pmatrix}224\\-420\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
The magnitude of the given vector is \(476\).

Divide each component by \(476\). The scale factor is positive, so the arrow keeps its direction.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{8}{17}\\-\frac{15}{17}\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Choose a vector of the required length
examples.question: Find the vector with magnitude \(819\) that points in the same direction as \(\begin{pmatrix}-150\\-360\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
Divide the original vector by \(390\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{5}{13}\\-\frac{12}{13}\end{pmatrix}\) of length one.

Multiply the resulting vector by \(819\) for the required length.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}-315\\-756\end{pmatrix}\).

lessons.title: Position vectors and dividing a segment
lessons.summary: Find a midpoint or dividing point with a position vector and interpret positions beyond a segment.
lessons.objective: Find a midpoint or dividing point with a position vector and interpret positions beyond a segment.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to find a midpoint or dividing point with a position vector and interpret positions beyond a segment.
lessons.ideas:
For \(AC:CB=r:s\), the distance from A to C is the fraction \(\frac{r}{r+s}\) of the full distance.

Build both displacements from A, then find the scale factor in \(\overrightarrow{AC}=k\overrightarrow{AB}\) by comparing components.

A scale above \(1\) carries a point past the target. A negative scale places it on the other side of the start.
lessons.method:
Mark the start, target and finish. Treat the whole arrow as all the parts, not just the parts still to go. Multiply the displacement by the required fraction. Because this is a displacement from A, add the position of A afterwards to obtain the position from the origin. A midpoint is the ratio \(1:1\), so its position is also the mean of the two endpoint positions.

Draw both journeys with a single common tail. Compute the two differences. If a component of the longer journey is non-zero, dividing the corresponding components gives the scale factor. Check it in the other row. For a point between the ends, the scale factor is between zero and one.

Use the same journey calculation for a line extension. First build the displacement to the reference point and take the required multiple of it. A question may describe that multiple directly instead of giving lengths. Keep the origin separate from your starting point. Draw an approximate check of the answer. A factor between zero and one would leave the point on the original segment.
mistakes: The ratio of the distance already covered to the distance still to go is different from the fraction of the whole segment covered.
A ratio of position vectors compares arrows from the origin. Start both route arrows at A to compare how far along AB each point lies.
The factor scales the displacement between the points. Scaling the destination's position from the origin starts from the wrong place.

examples.title: Locate a point at a given ratio
examples.question: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}31\\-7\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}87\\-49\end{pmatrix}\). \(C\) lies on \(AB\) with \(AC:CB=5:2\). Give the position vector of \(C\).
examples.solution:
First calculate \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}56\\-42\end{pmatrix}\).

The fraction completed is \(\frac{5}{7}\). Add that fraction of the displacement to \(\begin{pmatrix}31\\-7\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}71\\-37\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Read a fraction along a segment
examples.question: Points \(A,B,C\) have positions \(\begin{pmatrix}36\\-12\end{pmatrix}\), \(\begin{pmatrix}48\\-48\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}46\\-42\end{pmatrix}\). Given \(\overrightarrow{AC}=k\overrightarrow{AB}\), find \(k\).
examples.solution:
The route vectors from \(A\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-30\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-36\end{pmatrix}\).

Divide a component of the first route by the corresponding component of the second. The other components give the same \(k\).

Answer: \(\frac{5}{6}\).

examples.title: Continue the line beyond the endpoint
examples.question: \(A\) and \(B\) have positions \(\begin{pmatrix}41\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}97\\-46\end{pmatrix}\). Find the position of \(D\) if \(\overrightarrow{AD}=\frac{5}{2}\overrightarrow{AB}\).
examples.solution:
\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}56\\-48\end{pmatrix}\). Multiply both components by \(\frac{5}{2}\).

Add the resulting displacement to the start at \(\begin{pmatrix}41\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}181\\-118\end{pmatrix}\).

lessons.title: Parallel lines and intersections
lessons.summary: Compare direction vectors, prove collinearity and find the meeting position of intersecting lines.
lessons.objective: Compare direction vectors, prove collinearity and find the meeting position of intersecting lines.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to compare direction vectors, prove collinearity and find the meeting position of intersecting lines.
lessons.ideas:
Two non-zero directions are parallel if one is a scalar multiple of the other.

Compare two non-zero displacements with a common starting point. If one is a scalar multiple of the other, the three points are collinear.

At a crossing, two journeys lead to exactly the same position. Their separate journey lengths can differ.
lessons.method:
Find the scalar from a pair of non-zero components. Apply it to the second entries and compare. A negative factor is allowed because it gives an antiparallel direction. If both first entries are zero, use the second entries. If only one first entry is zero, the vectors cannot be aligned unless one whole vector is zero.

From three positions, subtract the position of A from the other two. This gives \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and the displacement from A to C. Show the same multiplier works horizontally and vertically. Both arrows pass through A, so their parallel directions put all three points on one line. If the directions come from separate origins, parallel arrows alone cannot prove the lines coincide.

Write each position as start plus a multiple of its direction. Use different letters for the two multiples, such as \(r\) and \(s\). Equate first components and then second components. Solve the two scalar equations by elimination. Put one parameter into the route that uses it and use the other route to verify the final column vector.
mistakes: Parallel directions can point the opposite way. The test is a common scalar and the sign can be negative.
Comparing the distance from the origin alone does not test whether three points lie on one line.
Using one letter for both route parameters can force an extra condition. The positions agree, but the journey lengths need not.

examples.title: Compare corresponding components
examples.question: Find \(p\) such that \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-30\\p\end{pmatrix}\) are parallel.
examples.solution:
The first entries determine the scalar multiplier \(-3\).

Multiply the second entry \(-4\) by the same scalar.

Answer: \(12\).

examples.title: Check whether three points lie on a line
examples.question: \(A,B,C\) have positions \(\begin{pmatrix}49\\-6\end{pmatrix}\), \(\begin{pmatrix}69\\-26\end{pmatrix}\), \(\begin{pmatrix}61\\-17\end{pmatrix}\). Are the three points collinear?
examples.solution:
The routes from A are \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}20\\-20\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}12\\-11\end{pmatrix}\).

The ratios from the two components differ, so the two routes do not lie on the same line.

Answer: No, they are not collinear.

examples.title: Match positions on two lines
examples.question: One line contains the points \(\begin{pmatrix}54\\-11\end{pmatrix}+r\begin{pmatrix}9\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). The other contains \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{427}{6}\\-\frac{103}{3}\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(r\) at the intersection.
examples.solution:
Equate top and bottom entries separately. The displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{103}{6}\\-\frac{70}{3}\end{pmatrix}\) equals \(r\begin{pmatrix}9\\-4\end{pmatrix}-s\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\end{pmatrix}\).

Eliminate \(s\) by cross-multiplying its two coefficients. The compatible second parameter is \(\frac{8}{3}\).

Answer: \(\frac{5}{2}\).

lessons.title: Velocity, drift and collisions
lessons.summary: Combine or resolve constant velocities and decide whether moving objects reach the same position at the same time.
lessons.objective: Combine or resolve constant velocities and decide whether moving objects reach the same position at the same time.
lessons.before: Use this lesson to combine or resolve constant velocities and decide whether moving objects reach the same position at the same time.
lessons.ideas:
Velocity relative to the ground equals velocity relative to the water plus the water velocity relative to the ground.

For constant velocity, displacement equals elapsed time multiplied by velocity. Add the start to get a position.

A collision needs the same place at the same time, with a non-negative time counted from the given start.
lessons.method:
Draw a path between reference frames. First follow the object's movement through the water, then the movement of the water over the ground. The signed components show which direction the current helps and which direction it opposes. Work backwards by subtracting the current when the desired ground velocity is specified. The magnitude of the resulting velocity is its speed, if asked.

Check the units first. In \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), multiply by the time in seconds to get a displacement in metres. To compare two moving objects, use the time measured from the same instant. Read across the columns to get the equation in each coordinate. Use the row with a non-zero difference in velocities to identify the candidate collision time.

Solve the two component equations independently when both relative velocity components are non-zero. If the candidate times differ, the routes cross at different times or they do not meet. If a component has equal velocities, compare initial positions for that coordinate. Equal starts make that equation true for all times. Unequal starts make a meeting impossible.
mistakes: Adding speeds as plain numbers gives the wrong answer unless both velocities point the same way.
Equal horizontal positions only guarantee that the objects are level in one direction. Check the vertical positions too.
A crossing drawn without times shows a shared point on the routes. It cannot confirm both objects reach it together.

examples.title: Combine engine and current velocities
examples.question: A survey buoy has velocity \(\begin{pmatrix}16\\-70\end{pmatrix}\) relative to the water. The water flows at \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\63\end{pmatrix}\) relative to the ground. Both are in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the ground velocity.
examples.solution:
Follow the chain from buoy to water and water to ground. Add \(\begin{pmatrix}16\\-70\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\63\end{pmatrix}\).

Combine corresponding components, preserving their signs.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-7\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Move a starting position for a fixed time
examples.question: A raft starts at \(\begin{pmatrix}62\\0\end{pmatrix}\) metres. Its velocity relative to the water is \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\-75\end{pmatrix}\) and the current is \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\68\end{pmatrix}\) in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the position after 6 seconds.
examples.solution:
Ground velocity is \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-7\end{pmatrix}\). The displacement after 6 seconds is \(\begin{pmatrix}36\\-42\end{pmatrix}\).

Add the displacement to the starting position \(\begin{pmatrix}62\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}98\\-42\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Locate the meeting point
examples.question: Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}67\\-5\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}171\\-148\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-7\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. Find their meeting position.
examples.solution:
The equation for equal positions gives a common time of 13 seconds. Both components satisfy it.

Substitute that time into the first position vector. This gives \(\begin{pmatrix}67\\-5\end{pmatrix}+13\begin{pmatrix}11\\-7\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}210\\-96\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.title: End position minus start position
questions.prompt_html: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}104\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}108\\-8\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
questions.solution_html:
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}108\\-8\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}104\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Write the destination first. Check the direction by adding the result to the start position.

questions.title: End position minus start position
questions.prompt_html: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}111\\-11\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}122\\-17\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
questions.solution_html:
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}122\\-17\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}111\\-11\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Write the destination first. Check the direction by adding the result to the start position.

questions.title: Recover a starting position
questions.prompt_html: After 3 equal displacements of \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-3\end{pmatrix}\), a marker arrives at \(\begin{pmatrix}159\\-13\end{pmatrix}\). Give the starting position as a column vector.
questions.solution_html:
The total displacement is \(\begin{pmatrix}36\\-9\end{pmatrix}\).

The arrival position is the start plus total displacement, so subtract the displacement from \(\begin{pmatrix}159\\-13\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}123\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Work backwards from the final position using the opposite of the total displacement.

questions.title: Recover a starting position
questions.prompt_html: After 5 equal displacements of \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\-5\end{pmatrix}\), a marker arrives at \(\begin{pmatrix}170\\-36\end{pmatrix}\). Give the starting position as a column vector.
questions.solution_html:
The total displacement is \(\begin{pmatrix}40\\-25\end{pmatrix}\).

The arrival position is the start plus total displacement, so subtract the displacement from \(\begin{pmatrix}170\\-36\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}130\\-11\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Work backwards from the final position using the opposite of the total displacement.

questions.title: Combine two directions
questions.prompt_html: Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}142\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\144\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(5\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).
questions.solution_html:
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}710\\-20\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\144\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}712\\-164\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.

questions.title: Combine two directions
questions.prompt_html: Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}149\\-11\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-9\\151\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(4\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).
questions.solution_html:
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}596\\-44\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}-9\\151\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}605\\-195\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.

questions.title: End position minus start position
questions.prompt_html: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}161\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}167\\-10\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
questions.solution_html:
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}167\\-10\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}161\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Write the destination first. Check the direction by adding the result to the start position.

questions.title: End position minus start position
questions.prompt_html: The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}168\\-11\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}170\\-14\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).
questions.solution_html:
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}170\\-14\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}168\\-11\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html: Write the destination first. Check the direction by adding the result to the start position.

questions.title: Match the bottom components
questions.prompt_html: \(\begin{pmatrix}180\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(3\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\185\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}542\\-197\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).
questions.solution_html:
The bottom entry gives \(3p-(185)=-197\).

Add \(185\) and divide both sides by \(3\).

Answer: \(-4\).
questions.hint_html: Equate bottom entries. Solve the value before checking the other entry.

questions.title: Match the bottom components
questions.prompt_html: \(\begin{pmatrix}187\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(2\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\192\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}374\\-214\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).
questions.solution_html:
The bottom entry gives \(2p-(192)=-214\).

Add \(192\) and divide both sides by \(2\).

Answer: \(-11\).
questions.hint_html: Equate bottom entries. Solve the value before checking the other entry.

questions.title: Compare two vector expressions
questions.prompt_html:
1. Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(2\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).

    [3]

  2. \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(2\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\8\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-4\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\4\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\-1\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

The bottom entry gives \(2p-(8)=-4\).

Add \(8\) and divide both sides by \(2\).

Answer: \(2\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.

(b) Equate bottom entries. Solve the value before checking the other entry.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply the first vector by the stated scalar and subtract corresponding components.
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\4\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.title: Compare two vector expressions
questions.prompt_html:
1. Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}0\\6\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(3\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).

    [3]

  2. \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(3\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-3\\9\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}15\\-6\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\6\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

The bottom entry gives \(3p-(9)=-6\).

Add \(9\) and divide both sides by \(3\).

Answer: \(1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.

(b) Equate bottom entries. Solve the value before checking the other entry.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply the first vector by the stated scalar and subtract corresponding components.
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.title: Compare two vector expressions
questions.prompt_html:
1. Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}5\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\7\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(4\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).

    [3]

  2. \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(4\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\10\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}22\\-10\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}20\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\7\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}21\\-7\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

The bottom entry gives \(4p-(10)=-10\).

Add \(10\) and divide both sides by \(4\).

Answer: \(0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.

(b) Equate bottom entries. Solve the value before checking the other entry.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply the first vector by the stated scalar and subtract corresponding components.
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}20\\0\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.title: Compare two vector expressions
questions.prompt_html:
1. Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\8\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(5\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).

    [3]

  2. \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(5\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\11\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}31\\-16\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}30\\-5\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\8\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}32\\-13\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

The bottom entry gives \(5p-(11)=-16\).

Add \(11\) and divide both sides by \(5\).

1. \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\p\end{pmatrix}\) scaled by \(5\) and then decreased by \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\15\end{pmatrix}\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}52\\-40\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(p\).

    [3]

  2. Two vectors are \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}20\\-15\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\22\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(3\mathbf a-\mathbf b\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The bottom entry gives \(5p-(15)=-40\).

Add \(15\) and divide both sides by \(5\).

Answer: \(-5\).

(b)

Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}60\\-45\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\22\end{pmatrix}\) component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}59\\-67\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Equate bottom entries. Solve the value before checking the other entry.

(b) Do the multiplication before subtracting. A negative second component in the subtracted vector must be subtracted as a negative.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply the first vector by the stated scalar and subtract corresponding components.
Scale both components of \(\mathbf a\) to get \(\begin{pmatrix}60\\-45\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.title: End position minus start position
questions.prompt_html:
1. The position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-6\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}21\\-12\end{pmatrix}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\).

    [3]

  2. After 3 equal displacements of \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-3\end{pmatrix}\), a marker arrives at \(\begin{pmatrix}56\\-8\end{pmatrix}\). Give the starting position as a column vector.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}21\\-12\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract first components and then second components to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

The total displacement is \(\begin{pmatrix}33\\-9\end{pmatrix}\).

The arrival position is the start plus total displacement, so subtract the displacement from \(\begin{pmatrix}56\\-8\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}23\\1\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Write the destination first. Check the direction by adding the result to the start position.

(b) Work backwards from the final position using the opposite of the total displacement.

marking_criteria.description_html: Subtract the position vector of \(A\) from that of \(B\).
Start with the target position \(\begin{pmatrix}21\\-12\end{pmatrix}\). Subtract the start position \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).
Multiply the fixed displacement by the number of steps and subtract it from the final position.

    [3]

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Compare both components at once. Solving the linear equations gives \(r=2,\ s=1\).

Put either parameter back into its own expression to obtain \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-7\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-7\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

Equate top and bottom entries separately. The displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{20}{3}\\-\frac{106}{3}\end{pmatrix}\) equals \(r\begin{pmatrix}10\\-6\end{pmatrix}-s\begin{pmatrix}4\\7\end{pmatrix}\).

Eliminate \(s\) by cross-multiplying its two coefficients. The compatible second parameter is \(\frac{10}{3}\).

Answer: \(2\).

1. Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-22\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. After how many seconds do they meet?

    [3]

  2. Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-22\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. Find their meeting position.

    [3]

  3. Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}31\\-111\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-7\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\7\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. Do the robots meet after the timing starts?

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

At a meeting, \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-22\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

Using the vertical entries gives \(t=4\). Both equations agree because \(4\begin{pmatrix}0\\-6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-24\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(4\).

(b)

The equation for equal positions gives a common time of 4 seconds. Both components satisfy it.

Substitute that time into the first position vector. This gives \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}+4\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-10\end{pmatrix}\).

(c)

The vertical equation gives \(t=\frac{109}{14}\). The horizontal equation gives \(t=8\).

The times differ, so there is no collision.

Answer: No, the component times differ.
questions.hint_html:
(a) Compare both positions at the same time. One component can give a candidate time, but it must work in the other.

(b) A meeting position is the initial position plus the velocity multiplied by the common time.

(c) Two routes can cross without a collision. Test whether the times agree as well.

Find a common time from the component equations and substitute into one position vector.
The equation for equal positions gives a common time of 4 seconds. Both components satisfy it.
Equate the position expressions component by component and compare the candidate times.
The vertical equation gives \(t=\frac{109}{14}\). The horizontal equation gives \(t=8\).

questions.title: Plan two journeys through a current
questions.prompt_html:
1. A raft starts at \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}\) metres. Its velocity relative to the water is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\-12\end{pmatrix}\) and the current is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\9\end{pmatrix}\) in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the position after 3 seconds.

    [3]

  2. A floating instrument needs ground velocity \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Its current has velocity \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\19\end{pmatrix}\). All velocities are in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the required velocity relative to the water.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Ground velocity is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). The displacement after 3 seconds is \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-9\end{pmatrix}\).

Add the displacement to the starting position \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}9\\-7\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

Ground velocity equals the relative-to-water velocity plus \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\19\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract the current from \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-3\end{pmatrix}\), component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}14\\-22\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Add the velocity components first. Multiply by the time to get a displacement.

(b) Make the displayed component equation before deciding which direction to subtract.

marking_criteria.description_html: Add the two velocities, multiply by the elapsed time, then add the initial position.
Ground velocity is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). The displacement after 3 seconds is \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-9\end{pmatrix}\).
Subtract the current from the required ground velocity.
Ground velocity equals the relative-to-water velocity plus \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\19\end{pmatrix}\).

1. A raft starts at \(\begin{pmatrix}16\\-11\end{pmatrix}\) metres. Its velocity relative to the water is \(\begin{pmatrix}9\\-28\end{pmatrix}\) and the current is \(\begin{pmatrix}-5\\22\end{pmatrix}\) in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the position after 8 seconds.

    [3]

  2. A floating instrument needs ground velocity \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Its current has velocity \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\44\end{pmatrix}\). All velocities are in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the required velocity relative to the water.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Ground velocity is \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-6\end{pmatrix}\). The displacement after 8 seconds is \(\begin{pmatrix}32\\-48\end{pmatrix}\).

Add the displacement to the starting position \(\begin{pmatrix}16\\-11\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}48\\-59\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

Ground velocity equals the relative-to-water velocity plus \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\44\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract the current from \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\end{pmatrix}\), component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-47\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Add the velocity components first. Multiply by the time to get a displacement.

(b) Make the displayed component equation before deciding which direction to subtract.

1. Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}24\\0\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}164\\-98\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. After how many seconds do they meet?

    [3]

  2. Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}24\\0\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}164\\-98\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. Find their meeting position.

    [3]

  3. Two inspection robots have initial positions \(\begin{pmatrix}44\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) m and \(\begin{pmatrix}116\\-157\end{pmatrix}\) m. Their constant velocities are \(\begin{pmatrix}10\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\9\end{pmatrix}\) \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) respectively. Do the robots meet after the timing starts?

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

At a meeting, \(\begin{pmatrix}24\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}164\\-98\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

Using the horizontal entries gives \(t=14\). Both equations agree because \(14\begin{pmatrix}10\\-7\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}140\\-98\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(14\).

(b)

The equation for equal positions gives a common time of 14 seconds. Both components satisfy it.

Substitute that time into the first position vector. This gives \(\begin{pmatrix}24\\0\end{pmatrix}+14\begin{pmatrix}12\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}192\\-56\end{pmatrix}\).

(c)

The vertical equation gives \(t=12\). The horizontal equation gives \(t=12\).

The same non-negative time satisfies both equations.

Answer: Yes, at the same time.
questions.hint_html:
(a) Compare both positions at the same time. One component can give a candidate time, but it must work in the other.

(b) A meeting position is the initial position plus the velocity multiplied by the common time.

(c) Two routes can cross without a collision. Test whether the times agree as well.

Find a common time from the component equations and substitute into one position vector.

Equate the position expressions component by component and compare the candidate times.
The vertical equation gives \(t=12\). The horizontal equation gives \(t=12\).

questions.title: Plan two journeys through a current
questions.prompt_html:
1. A raft starts at \(\begin{pmatrix}23\\1\end{pmatrix}\) metres. Its velocity relative to the water is \(\begin{pmatrix}16\\-32\end{pmatrix}\) and the current is \(\begin{pmatrix}-5\\29\end{pmatrix}\) in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the position after 7 seconds.

    [3]

  2. A floating instrument needs ground velocity \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Its current has velocity \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\59\end{pmatrix}\). All velocities are in \(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the required velocity relative to the water.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Ground velocity is \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). The displacement after 7 seconds is \(\begin{pmatrix}77\\-21\end{pmatrix}\).

Add the displacement to the starting position \(\begin{pmatrix}23\\1\end{pmatrix}\).

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}100\\-20\end{pmatrix}\).

(b)

Ground velocity equals the relative-to-water velocity plus \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\59\end{pmatrix}\).

Subtract the current from \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\-3\end{pmatrix}\), component by component.

Answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}8\\-62\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Add the velocity components first. Multiply by the time to get a displacement.

(b) Make the displayed component equation before deciding which direction to subtract.

marking_criteria.description_html: Add the two velocities, multiply by the elapsed time, then add the initial position.
Ground velocity is \(\begin{pmatrix}11\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). The displacement after 7 seconds is \(\begin{pmatrix}77\\-21\end{pmatrix}\).
Subtract the current from the required ground velocity.
Ground velocity equals the relative-to-water velocity plus \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\59\end{pmatrix}\).
